paper_title: Looping Beyond Twice: A Scalable Recipe for Looped Mixture-of-Experts

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Looped Transformers introduce recurrent depth as a new scaling axis for LLMs: by repeatedly applying shared Transformer blocks, they increase effective depth without increasing parameter count. However, the benefits of looping remain unclear for large MoE LLMs under FLOPs-matched comparisons. The main reason is that the gains from additional iterations diminish quickly and can even turn into degradation, so the extra FLOPs spent on looping yield little substantial improvement. Consequently, prior work typically settles on two loops. We identify two main obstacles to scaling looped MoE. First, looping inherits and amplifies the curse of depth: hidden-state variance grows with each iteration as residual updates accumulate, which destabilizes deep recurrence and causes representations to drift. Second, looped MoE suffers from expert selection collapse: routers repeatedly select the same experts across loops, so extra iterations add computation without adding computational diversity. Guided by this diagnosis, we propose LOOM, built on a single principle: each loop should contribute new computation while keeping the recurrent state stable. LOOM stabilizes recurrence by scaling residual updates to bound variance growth and re-injecting the input embedding at every loop, and diversifies it through per-loop routers that engage different experts and a Looping Residual that carries earlier outputs forward. Experiments across 100M-1.7B models show stable scaling to 9-12 loops. Under near-iso-FLOP, the 700M model performs best at 5 loops, reducing perplexity from 18.36 to 16.54 and improving average zero-shot accuracy from 38.84% to 39.53% over the non-looped baseline. Without FLOP matching, the 1.7B model trained on 60B tokens peaks at 9 loops, reducing perplexity from 9.62 to 7.77 and improving average zero-shot accuracy from 42.4% to 47.7%. Code is available https://github.com/hed-ucas/LOOM.

sections.content: Looping Beyond Twice: Scalable Recipe for Looped Mixture-of-Experts Di He1,2,3, Pengxiang Li4, Da Chang1,2,3, Qingyan Meng2, Lu Yin5, Shiwei Liu6,7,8, 1Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, 2Peng Cheng Laboratory, 3University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, 4The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, 5University of Surrey, 6ELLIS Institute Tubingen, 7Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, 8Tubingen AI Center Corresponding author: sliu@tue.ellis.eu Looped Transformers introduce recurrent depth as new scaling axis for large language models (LLMs): by repeatedly applying shared Transformer blocks, they increase effective depth without increasing parameter count. However, the benefits of looping remain unclear for large MoE LLMs under FLOPs-matched comparisons. The main reason is that the gains from additional iterations diminish quickly and can even turn into degradation, so the extra FLOPs spent on looping yield little substantial improvement. Consequently, prior work typically settles on two loops. In this paper, we take closer look at why looped MoE fails to scale and identify two main obstacles. First, looping inherits and amplifies the curse of depth: hidden-state variance grows with each iteration as residual updates accumulate, which destabilizes deep recurrence and causes representations to drift. Second, looped MoE suffers from expert selection collapse: routers repeatedly select the same experts across loops, so extra iterations add computation without adding computational diversity. Guided by this diagnosis, we propose LOOM, built on single principle: each loop should contribute new computation while keeping the recurrent state stable. LOOM stabilizes recurrence by scaling residual updates to bound variance growth and re-injecting the input embedding at every loop, and diversifies it through per-loop routers that engage different experts and Looping Residual that carries earlier outputs forward. Experiments across 100M1.7B models show stable scaling to 912 loops, with the 1.7B model scaling to 9 loops. Under near-iso-FLOP, the 700M model performs best at 5 loops, reducing perplexity from 18.36 to 16.54 and improving average zero-shot accuracy from 38.84% to 39.53% over the non-looped baseline. Without FLOP matching, the 1.7B model trained on 60B tokens peaks at 9 loops, reducing perplexity from 9.62 to 7.77 and improving average zero-shot accuracy from 42.4% to 47.7%. Code: LOOM Figure 1. Loop-depth scaling of LOOM. Left: under near-iso-FLOP budget, LOOM achieves its best performance near 5 loops. Right: without FLOP matching, the 1.7B model scales to 9 loops, with substantial performance improvements. 1 Looping Beyond Twice: Scalable Recipe for Looped Mixture-of-Experts 1. Introduction Looped Transformers scale the computational depth of LLMs by repeatedly applying shared Transformer blocks, increasing effective depth without increasing parameters (Dehghani et al., 2018; Giannou et al., 2023; Saunshi et al., 2025; Geiping et al., 2025). Unlike conventional depth scaling, looping introduces an additional scaling axis orthogonal to model size and training data (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022). Recent studies demonstrate that recurrent depth improves algorithmic computation (Giannou et al., 2023), length generalization (Fan et al., 2025), and latent reasoning (Saunshi et al., 2025; Geiping et al., 2025; Hao et al., 2024), establishing looped computation as promising direction for LLM scaling. MoE architectures offer natural pathway for extending looped computation. By activating only sparse subset of experts per token, MoE models provide additional computation capacity for recurrent refinement under fixed budget (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022). However, current looped MoE systems struggle to benefit from deeper recurrence: increasing the number of loops often leads to loss degradation rather than further improvements. Beyond this regime, additional iterations yield diminishing returns. This has raised concerns about the practical benefits of looped MoE under matched FLOPs, since further increasing the number of loops mainly adds computation without corresponding performance gain. Consequently, existing approaches often limit recurrence to two iterations (Gao et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Lab et al., 2026). Figure 2. LOOM architecture. An -layer MoE block is reused for loops, with λ as scalar hyperparameter. At layer of loop t, γ = λ/(H denotes the Looping Residual, and Rt ) controls embedding re-injection, EMAt ) scales residual updates, gt = λ/(t denotes the router. To understand why deeper recurrence fails to pay off, we investigate the root causes of this limitation and identify two main obstacles to scaling looped MoE. First, looping amplifies the curse of depth (Sun et al., 2025): repeatedly reusing shared Transformer blocks causes residual accumulation and activation variance growth, as shown in Figure 3, which makes hidden states drift and destabilizes optimization in deep recurrence. Second, looped MoE suffers from expert selection collapse: shared routers produce nearly invariant expert assignments across loops, so later iterations repeatedly activate similar experts instead of refining earlier representations (shown in Figure 4). As result, increasing loop depth adds computation without adding useful computation. This reveals the central challenge of deep looped MoE: Is there an effective way to improve cross-loop information flow in looped MoE, so that recurrence can scale well beyond two iterations? To answer this question, we propose LOOM, built on single principle: each loop should contribute new computation while 2 Looping Beyond Twice: Scalable Recipe for Looped Mixture-of-Experts keeping the recurrent state stable. LOOM realizes this principle along two complementary axes, each targeting one of the obstacles identified above. Diversifying recurrence. To counter expert selection collapse, LOOM equips each loop with its own router, so that different iterations engage different subsets of experts rather than repeatedly activating the same ones. To make these diverse computations build on one another, LOOM further introduces Looping Residual, which carries the outputs of earlier loops forward so that later iterations can refine previous representations rather than overwrite them. Stabilizing recurrence. To counter the curse of depth, LOOM adopts residual scaling (Sun et al., 2025; Noci et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2026a), scaling the output of each attention and MoE block by γ = λ/(H ). This bounds residual accumulation and keeps signal propagation stable as the number of loops grows. In addition, to prevent deep recurrence from diluting input information and causing latent drift, LOOM re-injects the input embedding at each iteration (Geiping et al., 2025). To adapt this technique to looped MoE, we recalibrate the injected embedding at step with gt = λ/(t ), so that the anchoring signal remains well-scaled across iterations. Together, these components enable shared experts to progressively refine representations across loops, allowing LOOM to scale recurrence well beyond two iterations without routing collapse or recurrent degradation. Our main contributions are as follows: ❶ We identify two main obstacles that prevent looped MoE from scaling beyond two iterations: the curse of depth, in which residual accumulation causes variance growth and latent drift, and expert selection collapse, in which shared routers assign nearly identical experts across loops. ❷ We propose LOOM, principled recipe for deep looped MoE built on single design principle: each loop should contribute new computation while keeping the recurrent state stable. LOOM stabilizes recurrence through residual scaling and embedding re-injection, and diversifies recurrence through loop-specific routers and Looping Residual. ❸ Experiments across model scales from 100M to 1.7B parameters and up to 60B training tokens show that LOOM scales to 912 loops, and that the 1.7B model scales to 9 loops. Notably, under matched FLOPs, LOOM scales looping to 5 iterations while consistently achieving lower loss, providing strong evidence that recurrent depth is genuine and compute-efficient scaling axis for MoE LLMs. 2. Related Work Looped models. Looped LLMs reuse the same Transformer blocks along the depth axis, increasing effective depth without increasing parameter count. This idea traces back to Universal Transformer (Dehghani et al., 2018) and ALBERT (Lan et al., 2019). Recent studies demonstrate the potential of recurrent computation in dense Transformers: Geiping et al. (2025) show that test-time looping improves language models; Saunshi et al. (2025) connect recurrence with latent-space reasoning; and Fu et al. (2026), Wang et al. (2026a), and Movahedi et al. (2026) enable deeper recurrence through stabilization, residual scaling, and fixed-point formulations. HRM and TRM further explore recursive architectures for iterative reasoning (Wang et al., 2025a; Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2025). Chain-of-Experts studies iterative expert computation within each layer rather than recurrently reusing an entire shared MoE block (Wang et al., 2025b). Extending recurrent computation to sparse MoEs introduces additional challenges due to routing dynamics and cross-loop information propagation. Stability in deep residual stacks. Deep recurrence increases effective depth but can amplify residual dynamics, causing activation instability and loss degradation. Noci et al. (2022) show that rank collapse of token representations causes vanishing gradients in Transformers and can be prevented by scaling residual branches, while Sun et al. (2025) identify the curse of depth in LLMs, where Pre-LN variance growth renders deeper layers nearly identity mappings and propose 1/( l) to scale down the residual. To address this, Mix-LN (Li et al., 2024) applies Post-LN to earlier layers and Pre-LN to deeper layers. Another line of work redesigns the residual pathway itself: mHC (Xie et al., 2025) constrains the residual mixing matrices of hyper-connections to doubly stochastic manifold to restore the identity-mapping property and stabilize large-scale training, and Attention Residuals (Team et al., 2026) replace fixed additive accumulation with attention over earlier layer outputs, allowing each layer to selectively aggregate previous representations. Residual scaling has also been applied to recurrent models: Wang et al. (2026a) introduce loop-aware factor λ/(H ), and Movahedi et al. (2026) combine residual scaling with inter-loop mixing. Input re-injection further alleviates representation drift (Geiping et al., 2025). These techniques lay the foundation for stabilizing deep recurrence and motivate their adaptation to looped MoE. Looped MoE. Sparse gating enables MoE models to scale parameter capacity under limited computation, but introduces additional challenges for recurrent computation, particularly in expert routing and cross-loop information propagation (Shazeer 3 Looping Beyond Twice: Scalable Recipe for Looped Mixture-of-Experts Figure 3. Only Res Scale and Only Embed Inject add residual scaling and embedding re-injection, respectively, to Native, with no other modifications. (a) Training loss. (b) Activation variance during training. (c) Activation variance across recurrent iterations. et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022). Existing recurrent MoE studies have explored limited forms of recurrence. MoEUT extends Universal Transformer with MoE layers rather than stabilizing deep full-block recurrence (Csordas et al., 2024); Chain-of-Experts iterates experts within layers instead of reusing shared MoE block (Wang et al., 2025b); SMELT studies compute-matched MoE looping and identifies two loops as best (Wang et al., 2026b). LoopMoE introduces iteration-adaptive normalization, while Lee et al. (2026) study recurrent MoE models with varying expert utilization but maintain effective depth by reducing layers as loop counts increase (Chen et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026). These approaches demonstrate the potential of recurrent MoE, but scalable deep recurrence under fixed architecture remains underexplored. 3. Methodology Overview. LOOM repeatedly applies an -layer, pre-norm MoE decoder. Each loop applies layers ℓ = 1, 2, . . . , in order and repeats this walk for passes. The attention and expert weights are shared across loops, whereas each loop has its own routers. Removing embedding re-injection from LOOM increases validation perplexity from 18.62 to 26.05 at = 9  (Table 5)  , supporting its complementary role in anchoring recurrent states alongside residual scaling. 3.2. Diversifying computation across loops Loop-specific routers. Deep recurrence should enable successive loops to perform complementary computations. However, sharing routers across loops can produce nearly invariant expert selections, leading to expert selection collapse and limiting the benefits of additional iterations. LOOM addresses this limitation through loop-specific routing with shared experts: each layer uses separate router for each loop, while its expert weights remain shared. This decouples routing decisions across iterations, enabling different stages of recurrence to access different expert combinations without replicating expert parameters. Figure 4 provides two complementary observations: (i) lower cross-loop cosine similarity of expert-load distributions and (ii) greater variation in expert loads across loops. Together, these observations support more diverse expert utilization, prerequisite for complementary computation across recurrent iterations. Looping Residual. Loop-specific routers diversify computation across iterations, while progressive refinement additionally requires effective reuse of earlier computations. Training with segmented backpropagation LOOM uses segmented backpropagation, dividing the recurrent loops into consecutive segments of at most = 3 loops. Each segment receives supervision from language-modeling loss at its final loop, with gradients restricted to that segment. Figure 5 compares this strategy with backpropagation through all loops on the 350M model, highlighting two benefits. ❶ Lower memory consumption and faster training. From = 3 to = 12, segmentation maintains peak memory near 12.6 GiB, whereas unsegmented memory increases from 12.5 to 19.3 GiB. At = 12, the reported training time decreases from 26.1 to 12.6 hours. ❷ Improved stability and performance. Segmented runs achieve lower evaluation loss and higher average accuracy across seven downstream tasks. At = 9, the unsegmented run exhibits severe degradation, with evaluation loss reaching approximately 4.4 and average accuracy falling to approximately 34%. These benefits in speed and stability motivate using segmented backpropagation with K=3 by default in LOOM. Detailed comparisons in Table 6 further support using segmented backpropagation by default in LOOM. Algorithm 1 summarizes the forward computation and segmented training procedure of LOOM. 4. Each loop applies layers ℓ = 1, 2, . . . , in order and repeats this walk for passes. We count multiplyadds in units of d2 per token per stacked layer. With I=d, grouped-query qkv costs 3d2, causal SDPA costs 2d2, and oproj costs 1d2, so attention is 6d2. Each routed SwiGLU expert is three dd maps and costs 3d2; experts therefore cost 3kd2. Over loops the unit is (H, k) = H(6 + 3k) = 3H(2 + k). (5) We choose top-k so that (H, k) f1 = 84 (the non-looped anchor). Table 2 reports the compute budget of each loop count together with the experimental results. Val.ppl falls from the non-looped Baseline through Loop4, so four loops already improve on Loop2, Loop3, and Baseline (no-loop). Loop5 and Loop6 then stay with Loop4 rather than slipping. This already extends well beyond the two-loop setting adopted by prior looped models (Gao et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Lab et al., 2026). 4.2.2. NON-ISO-FLOP LOOP EXPERIMENTS Table 3 supports two conclusions. ❶ The complete recipe enables stable depth scaling. Across both model scales, LOOM remains stable under deeper recurrence and improves validation perplexity and downstream accuracy over the width-matched non-looped baselines. ❷ Relaxing the compute constraint favors deeper recurrence. Although performance gains gradually saturate, the highest seven-task average is attained at 12 loops in this sweep, extending beyond the preferred depth under the near-iso-FLOP setting in Section 4.2.1. 8 Looping Beyond Twice: Scalable Recipe for Looped Mixture-of-Experts Table 4. No tech. loops the unmodified backbone without additional techniques and rapidly becomes unstable as recurrence deepens. ❷ Residual scaling alone does not ensure stability. Res. scale adds only residual scaling; it mitigates perplexity degradation but still encounters unrecoverable loss spikes at larger loop counts. ❸ Embedding re-injection alone cannot sustain deep recurrence. Embed inject adds only embedding re-injection and exhibits substantial degradation as loop depth increases. All three underperform the non-looped baselines even at shallow recurrence, supporting the effectiveness of the combined mechanisms in LOOM for translating additional recurrent computation into performance gains. 4.2.3. SCALING UP TRAINING To evaluate LOOM at larger scale, we train 1.7B-parameter model on 60B tokens. Table 4 highlights two findings. ❶ Stability in large-scale training. The 1.7B-parameter LOOM remains stable over 60B training tokens. Nine loops perform best, at an unrolled scale of roughly 15B parameters (1.7B 9), achieving 7.77 validation perplexity and 47.7% average zero-shot accuracy. ❷ Scalability with model size. The same framework extends from 100M and 350M to 1.7B parameters without changing its loop-specific hyperparameters, while retaining the benefits of recurrent computation. At the 1.7B scale, nine loops reduce perplexity from 9.62 to 7.77 and improve average accuracy from 42.4% to 47.7% over the non-looped baseline. These results demonstrate the scalability of LOOM as MoE parameter counts increase. 4.3. Ablation 4.3.1. COMPONENT ABLATION Table 5 ablates components of the 350M, 9-loop LOOM model at step 5,000, supporting two design principles. ❶ Stable recurrent states are essential for deep looping. Removing residual scaling, embedding re-injection, or MoE RMSNorm substantially increases perplexity and reduces average downstream accuracy, underscoring the need to control residual accumulation, preserve input information, and regulate activation magnitudes under repeated block reuse. ❷ Effective recurrence benefits from computational diversity and information preservation. Removing per-loop routing or the Looping Residual worsens both metrics, supporting their roles in diversifying expert computation and retaining information across iterations. Together, these results support our central claim: scaling recurrent depth requires stable hidden states and useful computation from successive loops. 4.3.2. SEGMENTED BACKPROPAGATION LOOM adopts segmented backpropagation with segment length K=3, detaching the hidden state between segments to restrict gradient propagation to the current segment. Table 6 shows that segmentation improves training stability, validation perplexity, and average downstream accuracy relative to full backpropagation. The comparison holds the architecture, training data, optimizer, and global batch size fixed. For the deepest full-backpropagation runs, the training micro-batch 9 Looping Beyond Twice: Scalable Recipe for Looped Mixture-of-Experts is reduced to fit the memory budget; these runs are therefore not matched to the segmented runs in activation memory. By bounding the backward graph within each segment, segmentation limits activation storage while preserving forward information across loops, supporting stable training at greater recurrence depths. These findings motivate its use as the default training strategy in the non-iso-FLOP experiments. Table 6. Conclusion This paper presents LOOM, scalable recipe for extending recurrent depth in MoE LLMs beyond the commonly used two-loop regime. Our analysis identifies hidden-state variance growth and expert selection collapse as key obstacles to deeper recurrence. LOOM addresses these obstacles through residual scaling and embedding re-injection to stabilize recurrent states, together with per-loop routers and Looping Residual to diversify expert computation and preserve information across iterations. Experiments spanning approximately 100M to 1.7B parameters and up to 60B training tokens show stable scaling to 912 loops, with the 1.7B model scaling to 9 loops. Under matched training FLOPs, LOOM scales to five loops while consistently achieving lower loss, providing evidence that recurrent depth offers compute-efficient scaling axis for MoE language models.
